interest: This file offers historians exceptional insight into the complex, contested politics of cultural heritage, restitution, and historical memory in East Asia immediately following World War II. It vividly illuminates the bureaucratic clash within the U.S. government between the State Department's support for Allied restitution—particularly for devastated nations like China, the Philippines, and the Netherlands—and the War Department's realpolitik desire to preserve Japanese goodwill and minimize occupation burdens. Furthermore, the papers concerning Masajiro Takigawa's unpublished galley-proof history of Manchukuo provide a fascinating microhistory of post-colonial Northeast Asia during the Chinese Civil War, showing how American diplomats and the Library of Congress secured and preserved valuable puppet-state historical documentation while deflecting Chinese Nationalist attempts at extra-legal confiscation.
overview: State Department decimal file 894.412 (covering December 1945 to August 1948) documents United States policy and diplomatic actions concerning historical relics, manuscripts, and the restitution and replacement of cultural property associated with wartime Japan. The file centers on three distinct episodes: first, diplomatic exchanges in December 1945 between Washington, the U.S. mission in Bangkok, and SCAP regarding the identification and return of a sacred, seven-layered Buddhist relic transferred from Siam to Japan under wartime duress; second, an in-depth March 1948 policy memorandum analyzing inter-agency disputes within the Far Eastern Commission (FEC) and SANACC over policy paper SFE 202/2 ('Replacement of Cultural Objects'), pitting the State Department's advocacy for Asian Allies' cultural restitution against the Army's Civil Affairs Division (CAD); and third, a protracted May–August 1948 dispute in Peiping involving Consul General O. Edmund Clubb, who sheltered an unpublished Japanese galley-proof manuscript of 'Ten Years History of Manchoukuo' by Professor Masajiro Takigawa from confiscation by Chinese Nationalist authorities, enabling its microfilming by the Library of Congress before returning the original to its Japanese custodians.

subfiles.about: The State Department directs the U.S. political adviser in Bangkok to ascertain the Siamese government's wishes regarding the return of a sacred Buddha relic taken to Japan during World War II.
subfiles.summary: Acting Secretary of State Dean Acheson informs the U.S. political adviser in Bangkok that the former Siamese counselor in Tokyo requested the safekeeping and return of a sacred relic of Buddha brought to Japan during the war under alleged Japanese duress. While the Japanese Government claimed the relic was a voluntary gift, SCAP placed it in temporary safekeeping. Acheson instructs the Bangkok mission to consult the Siamese government and advise whether the relic should be repatriated.
subfiles.title: Telegram from Acting Secretary of State Acheson to Bangkok on Siamese Buddha Relic

subfiles.about: The U.S. mission in Bangkok reports that the Thai Government formally requests the return from Japan of the sacred Buddha relic given under duress.
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost (U.S. Chargé d'Affaires, Bangkok)
subfiles.summary: In response to the State Department's inquiry, Charles W. Yost reports that the Thai Government strongly desires the return from Japan of the sacred relic of the Buddha. The Thai authorities state that the relic was surrendered under wartime duress and emphasize its immense religious significance to the Thai population. The sub-file includes the Department's central records replacement cover sheet and duplicate telegram copies.
subfiles.title: Telegram from Yost (Bangkok) on Siamese Request for Return of Sacred Buddha Relic

subfiles.about: The Thai Government describes the seven-layered stupa housing the Buddha relic and insists that all layers be returned intact from Japan.
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost (U.S. Chargé d'Affaires, Bangkok)
subfiles.summary: Charles W. Yost transmits detailed information from the Siamese Government specifying that the sacred relic of the Buddha taken to Japan is encased within seven nested layers of stupas, comprising rock, iron, two layers of bronze, silver, gold, and crystal. The Siamese Government formally requests the return of the holy relic with all seven protective layers intact. This telegram was repeated directly to Tokyo for SCAP's information.
subfiles.title: Telegram from Yost (Bangkok) Detailing Seven Stupa Layers of Buddha Relic

subfiles.about: An internal memorandum examines inter-agency disagreements over policy paper SFE 202/2 regarding the replacement of cultural objects looted and destroyed by Japan.
subfiles.from: Robert A. Fearey (Office of Northeast Asian Affairs)
subfiles.summary: Robert A. Fearey summarizes the ongoing stalemate in the Far Eastern Commission (FEC) and the State-Army-Navy-Air Force Coordinating Committee (SANACC) concerning the proposed cultural replacement program for Japan. Fearey systematically refutes five objections raised by the Army's Civil Affairs Division (CAD), which had argued that replacing lost Allied cultural property would alienate Japanese goodwill, overburden SCAP, establish dangerous precedents, bias claims, and worsen inflation. Rejecting CAD's position as cynical and unsound, Fearey recommends maintaining the State Department's support for Allied restitution rights and forwarding a split report to SANACC.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from Fearey to Allison on State Department Position on Replacement of Cultural Objects (SFE 202/2)
subfiles.to: John M. Allison (Office of Northeast Asian Affairs)

subfiles.about: Consul General Clubb transmits an unpublished Japanese galley-proof manuscript on Manchukuo's history to Washington, recommending it be microfilmed before return.
subfiles.from: O. Edmund Clubb (American Consul General, Peiping)
subfiles.summary: Consul General O. Edmund Clubb transmits a copy of 'Ten Years History of Manchoukuo,' an unpublished galley-proof work written by Professor Masajiro Takigawa of Kengoku University. Clubb explains that the manuscript was entrusted to consulate translator Shigeki Sakimura for return to Japan, but Chinese Nationalist authorities in Mukden and Peiping demanded its surrender under the pretext of safeguarding state secrets. Having rebuffed Chinese municipal demands, Clubb suggests the State Department review and microfilm the valuable historical work before returning it to Sakimura.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 113 from Clubb (Peiping) Transmitting Japanese Manuscript 'Ten Years History of Manchoukuo'

subfiles.about: Translator Sakimura details the authorship, provenance, and attempted police seizure of Takigawa's manuscript on Manchukuo.
subfiles.from: Shigeki Sakimura (Translator, American Consulate General, Peiping)
subfiles.summary: Shigeki Sakimura provides a detailed account of Professor Masajiro Takigawa's background as an ideological figure in Manchukuo and the director of its State Library who compiled extensive historical documentation. Sakimura describes receiving the galley sheets from Professor Sakae Shikata in Changchun to deliver to Tokyo, and lending them in Peiping to Mrs. Furukawa for historical research. He recounts being interrogated by Peiping police officers who attempted to coerce him into surrendering the document, an effort halted by the intervention of the American Consulate General.
subfiles.title: Memorandum by Sakimura on the Provenance and History of the Manchukuo Manuscript
subfiles.to: O. Edmund Clubb (American Consul General, Peiping)

subfiles.about: Mayor Ho Ssu-yuan requests that the American Consulate surrender the Manchukuo manuscript on behalf of Nationalist authorities in Mukden.
subfiles.summary: Mayor Ho Ssu-yuan of Peiping conveys an urgent telegram from the Political Affairs Commission of the President's Northeast Headquarters in Mukden regarding Takigawa's manuscript. Acting on information from a Japanese employee named Akira Mukai (Hsiang Chiu Chang), Nationalist authorities claim the manuscript contains vital state secrets and was illicitly brought to Peiping by consulate employee Shigeki Sakimura. The Mayor requests that Consul General Clubb deliver the manuscript to municipal authorities so it can be returned to Mukden.
subfiles.title: Translation of Letter from Peiping Mayor Ho Ssu-yuan to Clubb Requesting Surrender of Manuscript
subfiles.to: O. Edmund Clubb (American Consul General, Peiping)

subfiles.about: Consul General Clubb refuses to deliver the Manchukuo manuscript to Peiping municipal authorities without specific identification and legal justification.
subfiles.from: O. Edmund Clubb (American Consul General, Peiping)
subfiles.summary: Replying to Mayor Ho Ssu-yuan, Consul General O. Edmund Clubb states that the manuscript in his possession shows no indication of being an official or secret document of the puppet Manchukuo Government, noting it is printed galley material and essentially private property. Clubb confirms that translator Shigeki Sakimura obtained the manuscript legitimately from its rightful custodian. He declines to surrender the work unless the Chinese authorities properly identify the document by author and title and establish a valid legal basis for their request.
subfiles.title: Letter from Clubb to Mayor Ho Ssu-yuan Refusing Unsubstantiated Surrender of Manuscript

subfiles.about: The State Department reports that the Library of Congress has microfilmed Takigawa's manuscript and that the original is being returned to Peiping.
subfiles.from: Department of State (Acting Secretary of State / W. E. Jenkins)
subfiles.summary: The Department of State informs the American Consular Officer in Charge at Peiping that a preliminary examination of 'Ten Years History of Manchoukuo' revealed material of significant historical value containing no secret information. The manuscript was sent to the Library of Congress, which microfilmed it for historical research purposes and expressed gratitude. The original physical manuscript is returned under separate cover to the consulate for delivery back to Mr. Sakimura and its owner.
subfiles.title: Despatch from State Department to Peiping Consulate General on Microfilming of Manchukuo Manuscript
subfiles.to: American Consular Officer in Charge, Peiping

subfiles.about: Consul Touchette reports a renewed Chinese Nationalist request for the Manchukuo manuscript and urges its prompt return if microfilmed.
subfiles.summary: Consul Joseph W. Touchette notifies the Secretary of State that the Peiping Municipal Government has renewed its demand for the Takigawa manuscript on behalf of the Political Affairs Commission of the Northeast Bandit Suppression Headquarters, which claimed custody was needed for administrative reference. Touchette requests that if the manuscript has already been microfilmed in Washington, it be returned as soon as possible. He notes that the consulate is withholding an answer to the Chinese authorities pending instructions.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 268 from Touchette (Peiping) on Renewed Chinese Demand for Manuscript

subfiles.about: Secretary Marshall inquires whether the Peiping consulate objects to the Library of Congress microfilming the non-secret manuscript.
subfiles.summary: Secretary of State George C. Marshall informs the American Consulate General in Peiping that preliminary evaluation of Takigawa's manuscript disclosed no secret information or material of immediate operational interest to the Department. He reports that the Library of Congress wishes to microfilm the text, with the understanding that the Department will review the film prior to making it available to researchers. Marshall asks whether the consulate has any objection to this procedure.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 132 from Secretary of State Marshall to Peiping on Library of Congress Microfilming

subfiles.about: The Peiping Consulate General agrees to microfilming the manuscript and requests that the physical copy be returned to China.
subfiles.summary: Responding to Department Telegram No. 132, Consul Joseph W. Touchette informs the Secretary of State that the Consulate General in Peiping sees no objection to the proposed microfilming procedure by the Library of Congress. Touchette reiterates the recommendation that the physical manuscript be returned to Peiping upon completion of the filming so that it can be restored to its rightful custodian.
subfiles.title: Telegram from Touchette (Peiping) Concurring with Microfilming and Requesting Return of Manuscript
